additional_requirements: Functioning is not markedly impaired apart from the impact of the delusion(s) or its ramifications

S019.name: Delusions
S019.description: Fixed beliefs that do not change easily, even in the face of contradictory evidence.

subtypes.Persecutory Delusions: The false belief that one is being harmed or monitored by other people or organizations.
subtypes.Referential Delusions: The conviction that ordinary events, remarks, or behaviors have specific relevance to oneself.
subtypes.Grandiose Delusions: The false belief that one possesses special abilities, power, or fame.
subtypes.Erotomanic Delusions: The false belief that another person is in love with or has affection for them.
subtypes.Nihilistic Delusions: A destructive or negative conviction that the world is ending or that a major catastrophe will occur.
subtypes.Somatic Delusions: The baseless conviction that there is a serious abnormality with one's body or organs.
subtypes.Jealous Delusions: The conviction that one's spouse or romantic partner is being unfaithful without sufficient evidence.

symptom.disease_info: Delusional disorder is characterized by the presence of one or more persistent delusions lasting at least one month, in the absence of prominent hallucinations, disorganized thought, or marked negative symptoms seen in schizophrenia. Outside of the delusional beliefs, functioning is often relatively preserved and behavior may not appear obviously odd, which can delay recognition and treatment. The delusions tend to be non-bizarre or only moderately implausible, systematized, and fixed despite clear contradictory evidence, and are not better explained by mood disorders, substance use, or neurocognitive disorders. Onset is often in mid to late adulthood, and the course is typically chronic, with stressors, social isolation, or sensory and medical changes sometimes preceding or shaping the content of the delusional beliefs.

patient.personality: A cautious, routine-driven retiree who finds comfort in structure, quiet hobbies, and meticulous record-keeping, while privately worrying about the future.
patient.stressor: Roughly two years ago, Carmelia lost a close friend from church and community gardening, a woman she had relied on for daily phone calls and shared routines since her divorce. The loss intensified her longstanding worries about aging alone, safety, and what would happen if she became ill or dependent, leaving her clinging even more tightly to routines, lists, and the small collections she kept hidden at home. Over the subsequent year and a half, her attempts to explain and emotionally organize this bereavement and her fears gradually crystallized into a rigid, all-encompassing interpretation of events around her, which she began to defend vigorously despite gentle challenges from fellow volunteers and church members. Her adult daughter ultimately brought her to psychiatric care after noticing that these firmly held explanations were driving conflicts with neighbors, disrupting her work at the garden and food pantry, and making it increasingly difficult to reason with her about everyday practical decisions.
patient.chief_complaint: “My daughter says I’m too stuck on certain beliefs and won’t listen when people tell me they can’t be true.”

S019.name: Delusions
S019.description: Fixed beliefs that do not change easily, even in the face of contradictory evidence.
S019.manifestation: Ever since my friend from church passed, I’ve become absolutely certain that the neighbors and some people from the garden group have a quiet arrangement to keep tabs on me—like when the porch light across the street blinks a certain way or the church bulletin has a phrase I’ve never used before, I know it’s about me and part of their plan to see how I’ll manage alone, and no matter how many times my daughter insists it’s just coincidence, I can’t shake what I know in my gut is going on.
